STRONGLY TRADITIONAL

The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers

The second chapter of a trilogy is the hardest to get right. It must deepen the stakes, expand the world, and darken the tone without resolution.……

Film · Theaters / Max / Amazon Prime August 6, 2026 Analyzed by VirtueVigil Editorial Team 10 min read
Woke Score
0.35
Traditional Score
24.99

9%
Score Margin
+25 TRAD
Overall Perspective

The second chapter of a trilogy is the hardest to get right. It must deepen the stakes, expand the world, and darken the tone without resolution. It must make the audience feel the weight of the journey. Peter Jackson's The Two Towers does all of this and more: it is, in many ways, the moral center of The Lord of the Rings.

The story splits into three threads. Frodo (Elijah Wood) and Sam (Sean Astin) continue their journey to Mordor, now guided by Gollum (Andy Serkis in a landmark motion-capture performance), a creature consumed by the Ring and torn between the remnants of his former self, Smeagol, and the corrosive influence that has devoured him for five hundred years. This thread is the psychological heart of the film: a meditation on temptation, mercy, and the terrible cost of bearing a burden no one should have to carry alone.

In Rohan, Aragorn (Viggo Mortensen), Legolas (Orlando Bloom), and Gimli (John Rhys-Davies) arrive to find King Theoden (Bernard Hill) reduced to a shell of himself, poisoned by the whispers of Grima Wormtongue (Brad Dourif), Saruman's agent. Gandalf (Ian McKellen), believed dead after the Mines of Moria, returns as Gandalf the White, frees Theoden from Saruman's grip, and leads the Rohirrim to the fortress of Helm's Deep for a last stand against Saruman's army of ten thousand Uruk-hai. The Battle of Helm's Deep remains one of the most extraordinary achievements in action cinema: a siege that earns every moment of its runtime through character stakes, tactical clarity, and emotional weight.

The third thread follows Merry and Pippin, who escape their Uruk-hai captors into Fangorn Forest, where they meet Treebeard, an Ent, a shepherd of the trees. The Ents' march on Isengard, the industrialized fortress of Saruman, is Tolkien's clearest ecological statement: nature rising in righteous fury against the machine that would devour it. It is not an ideological lecture. It is myth.

What makes The Two Towers exceptional within the VirtueVigil framework is that its traditionalism is not incidental. It is the framework's thesis statement brought to life. Tolkien was a devout Catholic who embedded his faith into the bones of Middle-earth. The moral universe of the story is Objective Good vs. Evil at every level: the free peoples of Middle-earth versus the forces of Mordor and Isengard. There is no moral ambiguity in this war. The villains are evil and the heroes, though flawed, are good.

Every major character arc embodies a traditional virtue. Frodo and Sam represent The Self-Sacrificing Hero in its most extreme form: two small hobbits walking into hell because no one else can. Sam's loyalty to Frodo is a kind of love that the modern world has largely forgotten: steadfast, selfless, and expressed through service rather than sentiment. Aragorn embodies The Reluctant Leader, accepting authority only because duty demands it. Theoden, once freed from Wormtongue's influence, becomes The Principled Patriarch restored: a king who prepares to die defending his people. Gandalf's return from death is Biblical Morality made literal: the resurrection of a guide who sacrificed himself for his companions.

The film contains only the faintest markers on the woke side of the ledger. Eowyn (Miranda Otto) chafes against her assigned role as the woman left behind while the men ride to war. But her arc is more complex than a simple Girl Boss narrative. She is not placed on the battlefield in this film; Theoden explicitly tells her she must lead the people in his absence, a role of profound responsibility. Her eventual turn to arms in Return of the King is earned through showing that her courage is equal to any man's, not through grievance. The Ents' destruction of Isengard could be read as an environmentalist parable, but Tolkien's anti-industrialism was rooted in a traditional love of the English countryside and a horror at the mechanized slaughter of World War I, not in contemporary climate politics.

On the traditional side, the ledger overflows. The Self-Sacrificing Hero (Frodo, Sam, Aragorn). The Principled Patriarch (Theoden, restored). Objective Good vs. Evil (the entire moral structure). Biblical Morality (Gandalf's resurrection, Sam's Christlike servanthood). Defense of the Innocent (Helm's Deep, explicitly). The Two Towers is the rare film that can be shown to a twelve-year-old and a philosophy professor with equal reward. It tells a story about courage, sacrifice, and the belief that good is worth fighting for, even when the darkness seems absolute. In a cultural landscape saturated with cynicism, that sincerity is revolutionary.
